</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Field">Field</span></h3>
<p>The <b>Field</b> is the <b>Play Area</b> or <b>Playmat</b> for a <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">Pokémon Trading Card Game</a> game or <a href="#Match">Match</a>. There are also <i>playmats</i> that players can use that define all the special location on the field. A field is roughly split in half with each player utilizing the half closest to them. Each player’s <a href="#Shuffle">shuffled</a> <a href="#Deck">deck</a> is placed face down on the upper right side of their respective half. The <a href="#Discard_Pile">Discard Pile</a> is located on the right side just below their deck. The <a href="#Active_Pokémon">Active Pokémon</a> (of which each player can only have one at a time) is placed in front of the player toward the upper center of their half of the field. Their <a href="#Bench">Bench</a> is directly in front of each player. No more than five Pokémon may occupy a given player’s Bench at the same time. Finally, six <a href="#Prize_card">Prize cards</a> are placed face down to the left side of the each player’s half of the field.
</p><p>Pokémon cards on both players' Active Spots and Benches are considered to be <b>In Play</b>.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Hand">Hand</span></h3>
<p>Generally held in the player’s hands, a player’s <b>hand</b> is the group of cards that only they are allowed to look at (not their opponent) and play from during their <a href="#Turn">Turn</a>. At the beginning of a <a href="#Match">Match</a>, players take seven cards from the top of their respective <a href="#Deck">decks</a> and places them into their hand. At the beginning of each player's turn, they take one card from the top of their respective decks and place it into their hand. Certain <a href="#Trainer_card">Trainer cards</a> and <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon cards</a> have <a href="#Attack">Attacks</a> or <a href="#Ability">Abilities</a> that may also allow a player to draw a card or cards from their respective deck. Notably, players always have a hand, even if that hand has no cards in it. This allows players to pay for costs that require discarding their hand even in such a case. <sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div id="AdThrive_Content_4_desktop" class="adthrive-ad adthrive-content adthrive-content-4 adthrive-ad-cls" style="min-height: 250px;"></div><h3><span class="mw-headline" id="HP">HP</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/HP_(TCG)" title="HP (TCG)">HP (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>HP</b> (Japanese: <span class="explain" title="エイチピー">ＨＰ</span> <i>HP</i>), short for <b>Hit Point</b> (Japanese: <b><span lang="ja" style="margin: 0px;">ヒットポイント</span></b> <i>Hit Point</i>), represents the health of each <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_(TCG)" title="Pokémon (TCG)">Pokémon</a> card. This is the amount of <a href="#Damage">Damage</a> it can take before being <a href="#Knocked_Out">Knocked Out</a>. This value is a multiple of 10. A Pokémon's damage is tallied up by way of damage counters, each counter representing 10 damage. For example, if a Pokémon with 120 HP has 3 damage counters, that is equivalent to 30 HP damage, with 90 HP still remaining for this Pokémon. If a Pokémon has lost all their HP (for instance, a Pokémon with 120 HP with twelve or more damage counters on it), it is Knocked Out. Once a Pokémon card is Knocked Out, it and all cards attached are sent to the discard pile, and the opponent takes one of their Prize cards.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Holofoil_card">Holofoil card</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Holofoil_(TCG)" class="mw-redirect" title="Holofoil (TCG)">Holofoil (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p>Also known as <b>Holographic Foil</b>, <b>Foil</b>, <b>Holo</b>, <b>Reverse-Holo</b>, <b>Reverse foil</b> or <b>Holographic</b> cards. They are identical to their normal counterpart aside from a Holofoil effect in the picture (<i>Holo</i>) or the card background (<i>Reverse-Holo</i>). A small amount of <a href="#Rarity">Rare</a> (<span class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/Rarity" title="Rare"><img alt="Rare" src="https://archives.bulbagarden.net/media/upload/thumb/b/b9/Rarity_Rare.png/21px-Rarity_Rare.png" decoding="async" loading="lazy" width="21" height="20" class="mw-file-element" srcset="https://archives.bulbagarden.net/media/upload/thumb/b/b9/Rarity_Rare.png/31px-Rarity_Rare.png 1.5x, https://archives.bulbagarden.net/media/upload/thumb/b/b9/Rarity_Rare.png/42px-Rarity_Rare.png 2x" data-file-width="3611" data-file-height="3461"></a></span>) cards within each <a href="#Expansion">expansion</a> are Holofoil. They may be pulled from <a href="#Booster_pack">Booster packs</a> as the rare card, but it is not guaranteed. They are rarer compared to non-Holofoil rare cards.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Knock_Out">Knock Out</span></h3>
<p>When a <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon</a>'s <a href="#Damage">Damage</a> equals or exceeds its <a href="#HP">Hit Points</a>, it is considered <b>Knocked Out</b>. Knocked Out Pokémon are placed face up in the player’s <a href="#Discard_Pile">Discard Pile</a> along with any other cards that were attached to it (such as <a href="/wiki/Energy_card_(TCG)" title="Energy card (TCG)">Energy cards</a>).
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Lost_Zone">Lost Zone</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Lost_Zone" title="Lost Zone">Lost Zone</a></i></dd></dl>
<p>The <b>Lost Zone</b> is an area considered to be a more advanced form of the <a href="#Discard_Pile">Discard Pile</a>. The Lost Zone was introduced in the <a href="/wiki/Platinum_(TCG)" title="Platinum (TCG)">Platinum</a> expansion. Cards moved to the Lost Zone are kept face-up, but unlike cards in the Discard Pile, are considered to be "outside" the <a href="#Field">Play Area</a> due to the fact they are not kept on the playmat if one is used. Cards moved to the Lost Zone are no longer considered to be in play, and cannot be retrieved by any means during gameplay. There are no card effects that can circumvent this.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Match">Match</span></h3>
<p>A game of <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">Pokémon Trading Card Game</a> is often called a <b>Match</b>.
</p>
<h3><span id="Play.21_Pok.C3.A9mon"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Play!_Pokémon">Play! Pokémon</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Play!_Pok%C3%A9mon" title="Play! Pokémon">Play! Pokémon</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>Play! Pokémon</b>, formerly known as <i>Pokémon Organized Play</i> or <i>POP</i>, is an official gathering of players of the <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">Pokémon Trading Card Game</a> and <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_games" title="Pokémon games">video games</a> to play, trade, and just generally have fun and learn about the games. It was formed by <a href="/wiki/The_Pok%C3%A9mon_Company_International" title="The Pokémon Company International">The Pokémon Company International</a> in 2003 to officially sanction and organize game play, including <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_League_(TCG)" title="Pokémon League (TCG)">Leagues</a>, <a href="#Tournament">Tournaments</a>, and prize systems.
</p>
<h3><span id="Pok.C3.A9mon_Checkup"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Pokémon_Checkup">Pokémon Checkup</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Checkup" title="Pokémon Checkup">Pokémon Checkup</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>Pokémon Checkup</b>, formerly the <b>between-turns step</b>, is the step between <a href="#Turn">turns</a> during which <a href="/wiki/Special_Condition_(TCG)" title="Special Condition (TCG)">Special Conditions</a> are checked. While this concept has existed since the start of the game, the name "Pokémon Checkup" was only introduced in <a href="/wiki/Sword_%26_Shield_(TCG)" title="Sword & Shield (TCG)">Sword & Shield</a>. After all Special Conditions and other effects have been checked, any Pokémon with 0 HP remaining are <a href="#Knock_Out">Knocked Out</a>. Then the next player's turn starts.
</p>
<h3><span id="Pok.C3.A9mon_League"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Pokémon_League">Pokémon League</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_League_(TCG)" title="Pokémon League (TCG)">Pokémon League (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p>A <b>Pokémon League</b>, often referred to simply as <b>League</b>, is a periodic gathering, typically weekly, of players of both the <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">Pokémon Trading Card Game</a> and <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_games" title="Pokémon games">Pokémon video games</a>. During a League session, players battle and trade for fun. It is typically not a structured <a href="#Tournament">Tournament</a>. However, each player can obtain an official <a href="/wiki/Play!_Pok%C3%A9mon#Registration" title="Play! Pokémon">Player ID</a>. Event organizers will upload player event play information to <a href="/wiki/Play!_Pok%C3%A9mon" title="Play! Pokémon">Play! Pokémon</a>, eventually resulting in <a href="#Current_rewards">minor prizes</a>.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Prize_card">Prize card</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Prize_card" class="mw-redirect" title="Prize card">Prize card</a></i></dd></dl>
<p>A <b>Prize card</b> (Japanese: サイド <i>Side</i>) is a card taken by a player for <a href="#Knock_Out">Knocking Out</a> one of their opponent's <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon</a>. At the start of the game, after drawing their initial hand and putting Pokémon into play, cards are taken from the top of the deck and set as player's Prize cards. Prize cards are laid face-down  and are unknown to both players. When using regular 60-card <a href="#Deck">decks</a>, six prizes are put down at the start of the game. However, three are put down if using 30-card <a href="#Half_Deck">Half Decks</a>, and four are put down if using  40-card prerelease decks. In a <a href="#Sudden_Death">Sudden Death</a> match, each player has one Prize card. When one player's Pokémon is Knocked Out, their opponent takes one of their own Prize cards and puts it into their <a href="#hand">hand</a>. Some effects can increase or decrease the number of Prize cards taken in this way. There are also effects that prevent players from taking any Prize card when Knocking Out a Pokémon, and those override any increase. Certain Special Pokémon cards, such as <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon-GX_(TCG)" title="Pokémon-GX (TCG)">Pokémon-GX</a> or <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_V_(TCG)" title="Pokémon V (TCG)">Pokémon V</a>, have text boxes that also allow the opposing player to take more Prize cards when they are Knocked Out, though this technically is not an effect that increases the number of Prize cards taken. Rarely, there are effects that can interact with the Prize cards, sometimes allowing a player to take theirs without Knocking Out a Pokémon. The first player to take all of their Prize cards <a href="#Winning">Wins</a> the game.
</p>
<div id="AdThrive_Content_5_desktop" class="adthrive-ad adthrive-content adthrive-content-5 adthrive-ad-cls" style="min-height: 250px;"></div><h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Public_information">Public information</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Public_information_(TCG)" title="Public information (TCG)">Public information (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>Public information</b> is information related to a <a href="#Match">Match</a> that is readily accessible by either player at any time, as long as such requests are not used for stalling. Public information includes all cards in play, such as: 1) <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon cards</a>, including any <a href="#Evolution_card">evolutionary</a> stages underneath <a href="#Active_Pokémon">Active</a> and <a href="#Benched_Pokémon">Benched Pokémon</a>; 2) <a href="#Energy_card">Energy cards</a> and <a href="#Trainer_card">Trainer cards</a> attached to Pokémon and in the <a href="#Field">Play Area</a>; 3) the cards in each player's <a href="#Discard_Pile">Discard Pile</a>; 4) the number of cards in a player's hand, and 5) the number of remaining <a href="#Prize_Card">Prize Cards</a> of each player.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Rarity">Rarity</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Rarity" title="Rarity">Rarity</a></i></dd></dl>
<p>On the bottom right corner of most cards, there is a small symbol that indicates its <b>Rarity</b> (how easy it is to find or obtain): <span class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/Rarity" title="Common"><img alt="Common" src="https://archives.bulbagarden.net/media/upload/thumb/8/8c/Rarity_Common.png/21px-Rarity_Common.png" decoding="async" loading="lazy" width="21" height="20" class="mw-file-element" srcset="https://archives.bulbagarden.net/media/upload/thumb/8/8c/Rarity_Common.png/31px-Rarity_Common.png 1.5x, https://archives.bulbagarden.net/media/upload/thumb/8/8c/Rarity_Common.png/42px-Rarity_Common.png 2x" data-file-width="3611" data-file-height="3461"></a></span> (Common), <span class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/Rarity" title="Uncommon"><img alt="Uncommon" src="https://archives.bulbagarden.net/media/upload/thumb/0/0f/Rarity_Uncommon.png/21px-Rarity_Uncommon.png" decoding="async" loading="lazy" width="21" height="20" class="mw-file-element" srcset="https://archives.bulbagarden.net/media/upload/thumb/0/0f/Rarity_Uncommon.png/31px-Rarity_Uncommon.png 1.5x, https://archives.bulbagarden.net/media/upload/thumb/0/0f/Rarity_Uncommon.png/42px-Rarity_Uncommon.png 2x" data-file-width="3611" data-file-height="3461"></a></span> (Uncommon), <span class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/Rarity" title="Rare"><img alt="Rare" src="https://archives.bulbagarden.net/media/upload/thumb/b/b9/Rarity_Rare.png/21px-Rarity_Rare.png" decoding="async" loading="lazy" width="21" height="20" class="mw-file-element" srcset="https://archives.bulbagarden.net/media/upload/thumb/b/b9/Rarity_Rare.png/31px-Rarity_Rare.png 1.5x, https://archives.bulbagarden.net/media/upload/thumb/b/b9/Rarity_Rare.png/42px-Rarity_Rare.png 2x" data-file-width="3611" data-file-height="3461"></a></span> (Rare). No symbol usually denotes a card that is part of a <a href="/wiki/Promotional_cards_(TCG)" title="Promotional cards (TCG)">Promotional set</a> or a <a href="#Basic_Energy_card">Basic Energy card</a>.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Reprinted_card">Reprinted card</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Reprinted_card" title="Reprinted card">Reprinted card</a></i></dd></dl>
<p>A <b>Reprinted card</b> is a card that has been printed in a previous <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">Pokémon Trading Card Game</a> set and has been included in a newer set. When a card is reprinted, older versions of a card can still be used in <a href="#Standard_format">Standard format</a> and <a href="#Expanded_format">Expanded format</a> <a href="#Tournament">Tournaments</a> provided the text of the card has not changed or if a single copy of a card with the current text is set aside for reference. This reference card cannot be actively used in the player's <a href="#Deck">deck</a>.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Rule_Box">Rule Box</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Rule_Box_(TCG)" title="Rule Box (TCG)">Rule Box (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p>A term introduced in the <a href="/wiki/Battle_Styles_(TCG)" title="Battle Styles (TCG)">Battle Styles</a> expansion, cards with a <b>Rule Box</b> collectively refer to those that have a text box that says the word "rule", such as <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon-EX_(TCG)" title="Pokémon-EX (TCG)">Pokémon-EX</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_BREAK_(TCG)" title="Pokémon BREAK (TCG)">Pokémon BREAK</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon-GX_(TCG)" title="Pokémon-GX (TCG)">Pokémon-GX</a>, <a href="/wiki/Prism_Star_(TCG)" title="Prism Star (TCG)">Prism Star</a> cards, <a href="/wiki/TAG_TEAM_(TCG)" title="TAG TEAM (TCG)">TAG TEAM</a> cards, <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_V_(TCG)" title="Pokémon V (TCG)">Pokémon V</a>, <a href="/wiki/Radiant_Pok%C3%A9mon_(TCG)" title="Radiant Pokémon (TCG)">Radiant Pokémon</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_ex_(TCG)" title="Pokémon ex (TCG)">Pokémon ex</a>. (Pokémon-ex from the <a href="/wiki/Pokemon_Trading_Card_Game#EX_Series" class="mw-redirect" title="Pokemon Trading Card Game">EX Series</a> do not have Rule Boxes.)
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Series">Series</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game#Wizards_of_the_Coast_sets" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">Pokémon Trading Card Game → Wizards of the Coast sets</a></i></dd></dl>
<p>A <b>Series</b> is a grouping of <a href="#Expansion">Expansion</a> sets based on a certain <a href="/wiki/Generation" title="Generation">Generation</a> of expansions, such as <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game#Generation_I" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">Generation I</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game#Generation_II" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">Generation II</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game#Generation_III" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">Generation III</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game#Generation_IV" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">Generation IV</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game#Generation_V" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">Generation V</a>, or <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game#Generation_VI" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">Generation VI</a>. Concurrently, series groupings are also taken from the title of the first expansion in that given grouping (itself typically based off of the title of a <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_games" title="Pokémon games">video game</a> release), such as the <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game#HeartGold_&_SoulSilver_Series" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">HeartGold & SoulSilver Series</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game#Black_&_White_Series" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">Black & White Series</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game#XY_Series" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">XY Series</a>.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Shuffle">Shuffle</span></h3>
<p><b>Shuffling</b> involves mixing the cards in a player’s <a href="#Deck">deck</a> or <a href="#Prize_Card">Prize cards</a> in a random and unpredictable way.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Special_Conditions">Special Conditions</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Special_Condition_(TCG)" title="Special Condition (TCG)">Special Condition (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p>A <b>Special Condition</b> (Japanese: <span class="explain" title="とくしゅじょうたい">特殊状態</span> <i>Special Condition</i>) is a result that some <a href="#Attack">Attacks</a> have. Specific attacks may cause the <a href="#Defending_Pokémon">Defending Pokémon</a> to be affected by at least one of the five Special Conditions: <i>Asleep</i>, <i>Burned</i>, <i>Confused</i>, <i>Paralyzed</i> and <i>Poisoned</i>.
</p><p>Unlike <a href="/wiki/Status_ailment" class="mw-redirect" title="Status ailment">status ailments</a> in the video games, Special Conditions are not necessarily mutually exclusive. Poisoned and Burned are recognized by placing a specific marker (known as <i>status counters</i>) on the afflicted Pokémon (and can be combined), while Asleep, Confused, and Paralyzed are recognized by rotating the Active Pokémon's card (thus it can only be affected by one of these at a time with the newest condition overriding the previous one).  Also unlike the video games, Special Conditions are healed upon an <a href="#Evolution_card">Evolution</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Lv.X_(TCG)" class="mw-redirect" title="Pokémon Lv.X (TCG)">level-up</a> or being switched out of the <a href="#Active_Pokémon">Active</a> position and placed on the <a href="#Bench">Bench</a>.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Sudden_Death">Sudden Death</span></h3>
<p>When both players achieve a win condition at the same time, a Sudden Death match occours to resolve the original match's winner. It follows the same rules of a regular match, but players only start with one <a href="#Prize_Card">Prize Card</a>.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Tournament">Tournament</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Play!_Pok%C3%A9mon#Local_Tournaments" title="Play! Pokémon">Play! Pokémon → Local Tournaments</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>Tournaments</b> are meant for both fun and practice. They are usually held in a gaming store or community center by a local <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_League_(TCG)#League_Leader" title="Pokémon League (TCG)">League Leader</a> or <a href="/wiki/Tournament_Organizer_(TCG)" title="Tournament Organizer (TCG)">Tournament Organizer</a>. They are often but not always free to enter. <a href="#Play!_Pokémon">Play! Pokémon</a> sanctioned tournaments are either single elimination, Swiss, or Swiss followed by single elimination rounds. Formal Play! Pokémon tournaments also include: <a href="/wiki/Play!_Pok%C3%A9mon#Prerelease_Tournaments" title="Play! Pokémon">Prerelease Tournaments</a>, <a href="/wiki/Play!_Pok%C3%A9mon#Battle_Road_Tournaments" title="Play! Pokémon">Battle Road Tournaments</a>, <a href="/wiki/Play!_Pok%C3%A9mon#City_Championships" title="Play! Pokémon">City Championships</a>, <a href="/wiki/Play!_Pok%C3%A9mon#State/Province/Territory_Championships" title="Play! Pokémon">State/Province/Territory Championships</a>, <a href="/wiki/Play!_Pok%C3%A9mon#Regional_Championships" title="Play! Pokémon">Regional Championships</a>, <a href="/wiki/Play!_Pok%C3%A9mon#National_Championships" title="Play! Pokémon">National Championships</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Play!_Pok%C3%A9mon#World_Championships" title="Play! Pokémon">World Championships</a>. Many tournaments also are divided into three <a href="/wiki/Play!_Pok%C3%A9mon#Age_divisions" title="Play! Pokémon">Age divisions</a>: <i>Junior</i> (roughly up to ten year olds), <i>Senior</i> (roughly 11 to 14 year olds), and <i>Master</i> (roughly 15 year olds and older).
</p>
<div id="AdThrive_Content_6_desktop" class="adthrive-ad adthrive-content adthrive-content-6 adthrive-ad-cls" style="min-height: 250px;"></div><h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Turn">Turn</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game#How_to_play" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">Pokémon Trading Card Game → How to play</a></i></dd></dl>
<p>A <b>turn</b> consists of the following for each player:
</p>
<ol><li>First, draw a card from the top of that player's <a href="#Deck">deck</a>.</li>
<li>Next, do any of the below actions in any order:
<ul><li>Attach one <a href="#Energy_card">Energy card</a> to one of that player’s Pokémon in play (either <a href="#Active_Pokémon">Active</a> or <a href="#Bench">Benched Pokémon</a>).</li>
<li>Play <a href="#Basic_Pokémon">Basic Pokémon</a> to that player's Bench.</li>
<li><a href="#Evolution_card">Evolve</a> any of that player's Pokémon in play.</li>
<li><a href="#Retreat_cost">Retreat</a> that player's Active Pokémon if the Active Pokémon can satisfy the <a href="/wiki/Energy_card_(TCG)" title="Energy card (TCG)">Energy card</a> retreat cost.</li>
<li>Play any <a href="#Trainer_card">Trainer cards</a> in that player's <a href="#Hand">hand</a> pertaining to the rules on each Trainer card and then typically placing that Trainer card face up in the player’s <a href="#Discard_Pile">discard pile</a>.
<ul><li>During the same turn, each player may play many Item cards or Pokémon Tool cards, but only one Supporter card and one Stadium card.</li></ul></li>
<li>Use any <a href="#Ability">Abilities</a> or <a href="#Pokémon_Power">Pokémon Powers</a> that appear on that player's Active or Benched Pokémon.</li></ul></li>
<li>Finally, <a href="#Attack">Attack</a> if that player has the appropriate <a href="#Energy_card">Energy card(s)</a> attached on that player's <a href="/wiki/Glossary_(TCG)#Active_Pokémon" class="mw-redirect" title="Glossary (TCG)">Active Pokémon</a>. Attacking <b>always ends</b> that player’s turn.</li></ol>
<p>The player to go first is not allowed to attack or play a Supporter card on their first turn.
Players alternate turns until one player <a href="#Winning">wins</a> the game.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Winning">Winning</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game#How_to_play" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">Pokémon Trading Card Game → How to play</a></i></dd></dl>
<p>Players can <b>Win</b> a <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">Pokémon Trading Card Game</a> in three different ways:
</p>
<ol><li>Take their <i><a href="#Prize_Card">six prize cards</a></i> by <a href="#Knock_Out">Knocking Out</a> their opponent's Pokémon by using various <a href="#Attack">Attacks</a> to reduce the opponent's <a href="#Hit_Points">HP to zero</a>;</li>
<li>If their opponent <i>runs out of Pokémon</i> on the field (which includes their <a href="#Active_Pokémon">Active Pokémon</a> and <a href="#Bench">Bench Pokémon</a>), or</li>
<li>If their opponent must draw a card from their <a href="#Deck">deck</a> at the beginning of their turn, but they have <i>run out of cards in their deck</i>.</li></ol>
<h2><span id="Pok.C3.A9mon_card"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Pokémon_card">Pokémon card</span></h2>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_(TCG)" title="Pokémon (TCG)">Pokémon (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>Pokémon cards</b> are the focus of the <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">Pokémon Trading Card Game</a>. The most common type of Pokémon card is a <a href="#Basic_Pokémon">Basic Pokémon</a>, but others include <a href="#Baby_Pokémon">Baby Pokémon</a>, <a href="#Evolution_card">Stage 1 and Stage 2 Pokémon</a>, <a href="#Restored_Pokémon">Restored Pokémon</a>, <a href="#Pokémon-EX">Pokémon-EX and M Pokémon-EX</a>, <a href="#Fossil_card">Fossil Pokémon</a>, and <a href="#Pokémon_LEGEND">Pokémon LEGEND</a>.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Ability">Ability</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Ability_(TCG)" title="Ability (TCG)">Ability (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p>An <b>Ability</b> is a <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon</a> power that typically trigger once or multiple times during a <a href="#Turn">Turn</a>, before a Pokémon attacks, or are active for as long as the Pokémon that has it is in play. With the release of <a href="/wiki/Black_%26_White_(TCG)" title="Black & White (TCG)">Black & White</a>, <a href="#Pokémon_Power">Pokémon Powers</a> (<a href="#Poké-BODY">Poké-BODY</a> and <a href="#Poké-POWER">Poké-POWER</a>) were combined into this single mechanic after the analogous element in the main <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_games" title="Pokémon games">video series games</a>.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Ancient_Trait">Ancient Trait</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Ancient_Trait" class="mw-redirect" title="Ancient Trait">Ancient Trait</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>Ancient Traits</b> are special effects given to certain Pokémon, starting in the <a href="/wiki/Primal_Clash_(TCG)" title="Primal Clash (TCG)">Primal Clash</a> expansion. They are not <a href="#Ability">Abilities</a>, and as such, effects that would prevent Abilities from activating do not apply to them.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Attack">Attack</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Attack_(TCG)" title="Attack (TCG)">Attack (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>Attacks</b> are skills on a <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon card</a> usable by the player's <a href="#Active_Pokémon">Active Pokémon</a> on the player's <a href="#Turn">Turn</a>, which are similar to <a href="#Move">moves</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_games" title="Pokémon games">video games</a>. Nearly every <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon card</a> has at least one attack. When players use an attack, that player's turn ends. Every attack has an attack cost, which is printed as energy symbols to the left of the attack name. A Pokémon card can only use an attack if it has enough <a href="#Energy_card">Energy</a> attached to it to pay for that attack's cost. Additionally, only Active Pokémon may use attacks, although players may attach energy to <a href="#Bench">Bench</a> Pokémon in order to get them ready to attack if and when they make a given Bench Pokémon their Active Pokémon. Finally, the first player in a <a href="#Match">Match</a> to have a <a href="#Turn">Turn</a> is not allowed to attack, although they may perform all other actions types.
</p>
<div id="AdThrive_Content_7_desktop" class="adthrive-ad adthrive-content adthrive-content-7 adthrive-ad-cls" style="min-height: 250px;"></div><h3><span id="Baby_Pok.C3.A9mon"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Baby_Pokémon">Baby Pokémon</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Baby_Pok%C3%A9mon#In_the_TCG" title="Baby Pokémon">Baby Pokémon</a></i></dd></dl>
<p>A <b>Baby Pokémon</b> (Japanese: ベイビィポケモン <i>Baby Pokémon</i>) is a type of <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon card</a> introduced in <a href="/wiki/Neo_Genesis_(TCG)" title="Neo Genesis (TCG)">Neo Genesis</a> to be treated as a <a href="#Basic_Pokémon">Basic Pokémon</a>. Baby Pokémon are pre-<a href="/wiki/Evolution" title="Evolution">evolved</a> forms of existing Basic Pokémon, such as <a href="/wiki/Pichu_(TCG)" title="Pichu (TCG)">Pichu</a> is to <a href="/wiki/Pikachu_(TCG)" title="Pikachu (TCG)">Pikachu</a>, and thus are able to evolve into their respective Basic Pokémon (which are then treated as <a href="#Evolution_Pokémon">evolved Pokémon</a>). Up to the <a href="/wiki/Skyridge_(TCG)" title="Skyridge (TCG)">Skyridge</a> <a href="#Expansion">Expansion</a>, the opponent was also forced to flip a <a href="#Coin">coin</a> when attacking a Baby Pokémon: if tails, the <a href="#Attack">Attack</a> would fail. As of the <a href="/wiki/EX_Sandstorm_(TCG)" title="EX Sandstorm (TCG)">EX Sandstorm</a> <a href="#Expansion">Expansion</a>, Baby Pokémon are officially Basic Pokémon, and instead have a Baby Evolution <a href="#Poké-POWER">Poké-POWER</a> to allow them to evolve into their respective Evolutions.
</p>
<h3><span id="Basic_Pok.C3.A9mon"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Basic_Pokémon">Basic Pokémon</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Basic_Pok%C3%A9mon_(TCG)" title="Basic Pokémon (TCG)">Basic Pokémon (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p>A <b>Basic Pokémon</b> (Japanese: たねポケモン <i>Seed Pokémon</i>) is a form of <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon</a> which does not <a href="/wiki/Evolution" title="Evolution">evolve</a> from any other Pokémon. A Basic Pokémon can be placed directly into play, either as the <a href="#Active_Pokémon">Active Pokémon</a> at the start of the game or as a <a href="#Benched_Pokémon">Benched Pokémon</a> any time during play. Some Basic Pokémon, such as <a href="/wiki/Mewtwo_(TCG)" title="Mewtwo (TCG)">Mewtwo</a>, do not evolve; some, such as <a href="/wiki/Bulbasaur_(TCG)" title="Bulbasaur (TCG)">Bulbasaur</a>, do; and some, such as <a href="/wiki/Pikachu_(TCG)" title="Pikachu (TCG)">Pikachu</a>, can evolve from Baby Pokémon either classified as a Baby Pokémon or with the Baby Evolution <a href="#Poké-POWER">Poké-POWER</a>. In these cases, Basic Pokémon that are evolved from Baby Pokémon or other Basic Pokémon are considered to be evolved Pokémon, but not Evolution Pokémon.  Most <a href="#Pokémon-EX">Pokémon-EX</a> and <a href="#Pokémon_V">Pokémon V</a> are Basic Pokémon, but their subtypes (e.g. Mega Evolution Pokémon-EX) are not.
</p>
<h3><span id="Evolution_Pok.C3.A9mon"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Evolution_Pokémon">Evolution Pokémon</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Evolution_(TCG)" class="mw-redirect" title="Evolution (TCG)">Evolution (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>Evolution Pokémon,</b> or <b>Evolution cards</b>, are types of <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon</a> that <a href="/wiki/Evolution" title="Evolution">evolve</a> from other Pokémon, mainly split into <a href="#Stage_1_Pokémon">Stage 1 Pokémon</a> and <a href="#Stage_2_Pokémon">Stage 2 Pokémon</a>. A Pokémon that has had another Pokémon card placed on it as an Evolution is considered an "evolved Pokémon". The player's <a href="#Active_Pokémon">Active Pokémon</a> and their <a href="#Benched_Pokémon">Benched Pokémon</a> can be evolved during their <a href="#Turn">Turn</a>, as long it is not the player's first turn or the turn when the Pokémon was put into play. An evolved Pokémon counts as one card while in play, regardless of how many Evolution stages it has.
</p>
<h4><span id="Stage_1_Pok.C3.A9mon"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Stage_1_Pokémon">Stage 1 Pokémon</span></h4>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Stage_1_Pok%C3%A9mon_(TCG)" title="Stage 1 Pokémon (TCG)">Stage 1 Pokémon (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>Stage 1 Pokémon</b> are placed onto <a href="#Basic_Pokémon">Basic Pokémon</a> (including those evolved from <a href="#Baby_Pokémon">Baby Pokémon</a>) and Stage 2 Pokémon are placed onto Stage 1 Pokémon. Pokémon that are resurrected from Fossils in the original mechanic, such as <a href="/wiki/Omanyte_(TCG)" title="Omanyte (TCG)">Omanyte</a> and <a href="/wiki/Kabuto_(TCG)" title="Kabuto (TCG)">Kabuto</a>, are Stage 1 Pokémon, as their respective Fossil Trainer cards, <a href="/wiki/Helix_Fossil_(TCG)" class="mw-redirect" title="Helix Fossil (TCG)">Helix Fossil</a> and <a href="/wiki/Dome_Fossil_(TCG)" class="mw-redirect" title="Dome Fossil (TCG)">Dome Fossil</a>, are classed as Basic Pokémon.
</p>
<h4><span id="Stage_2_Pok.C3.A9mon"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Stage_2_Pokémon">Stage 2 Pokémon</span></h4>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Stage_2_Pok%C3%A9mon_(TCG)" title="Stage 2 Pokémon (TCG)">Stage 2 Pokémon (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>Stage 2 Pokémon</b> are placed onto <a href="#Stage_1_card">Stage 1 Pokémon</a>. Some cards, such as <a href="/wiki/Rare_Candy_(TCG)" class="mw-redirect" title="Rare Candy (TCG)">Rare Candy</a>, allow the player to bypass a Stage 1 Pokémon by evolving a <a href="#Basic_Pokémon">Basic Pokémon</a> directly into a Stage 2 Pokémon.
</p>
<h4><span id="Mega_Evolution_Pok.C3.A9mon"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Mega_Evolution_Pokémon">Mega Evolution Pokémon</span></h4>
<p><b>Mega Evolution Pokémon</b> are a Evolutionary stage introduced in <a href="/wiki/XY_(TCG)" title="XY (TCG)">XY</a> <a href="#Expansion">expansion</a> featuring the <a href="/wiki/Mega_Evolution" title="Mega Evolution">Mega Evolution</a> and <a href="/wiki/Primal_Reversion" title="Primal Reversion">Primal Reversion</a> mechanics. These are also <a href="#Pokémon-EX">Pokémon-EX</a> and are meant to be played by evolving from basic Pokémon-EX. Doing so ends a players <a href="#Turn">Turn</a> immediately.
</p>
<h4><span id="Pok.C3.A9mon_BREAK"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Pokémon_BREAK">Pokémon BREAK</span></h4>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_BREAK_(TCG)" title="Pokémon BREAK (TCG)">Pokémon BREAK (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>Pokémon BREAK</b> were introduced in the <a href="/wiki/BREAKthrough_(TCG)" title="BREAKthrough (TCG)">BREAKthrough</a> <a href="#Expansion">expansion</a>. They are easily identified through the stylized golden Pokémon graphic. A BREAK card retains the attacks, Abilities, Weakness, Resistance, and Retreat Cost of its previous Evolution.
</p>
<h4><span id="Restored_Pok.C3.A9mon"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Restored_Pokémon">Restored Pokémon</span></h4>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Restored_Pok%C3%A9mon_(TCG)" title="Restored Pokémon (TCG)">Restored Pokémon (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p>A <b>Restored Pokémon</b> (Japanese: <span class="explain" title="ふくげん">復元</span>ポケモン <i>Restored Pokemon</i>) is a form of <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon</a> that is revived to life from a <a href="#Fossil_card">Fossil</a>. In order to play a Restored Pokémon, the player must first play the respective <a href="#Fossil_card">Fossil card</a>, search the bottom seven cards of their <a href="#Deck">deck</a> for the corresponding Pokémon, and then place it onto their <a href="#Bench">Bench</a>. This type of card was reintroduced with the above mechanic in the <a href="/wiki/Noble_Victories_(TCG)" title="Noble Victories (TCG)">Noble Victories</a> <a href="#Expansion">expansion</a>.
</p>
<div id="AdThrive_Content_8_desktop" class="adthrive-ad adthrive-content adthrive-content-8 adthrive-ad-cls" style="min-height: 250px;"></div><h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Fossil_card">Fossil card</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Fossil" title="Fossil">Fossil</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>Fossils</b> or <a href="#Restored_Pokémon">Restored Pokémon</a> can only be played on to a player’s <a href="#Bench">Bench</a> through the use of special <a href="#Trainer_card">Trainer cards</a>, such as <a href="/wiki/Cover_Fossil_(TCG)" class="mw-redirect" title="Cover Fossil (TCG)">Cover Fossil</a> and <a href="/wiki/Plume_Fossil_(TCG)" class="mw-redirect" title="Plume Fossil (TCG)">Plume Fossil</a> to play <a href="/wiki/Tirtouga_(TCG)" title="Tirtouga (TCG)">Tirtouga</a> and <a href="/wiki/Archen_(TCG)" title="Archen (TCG)">Archen</a>. In order to play a Restored Pokémon, the player must first play the respective Fossil card, search the bottom seven cards of their <a href="#Deck">deck</a> for the corresponding Pokémon, and then place it onto their <a href="#Bench">Bench</a>.
</p>
<h3><span id="Pok.C3.A9-BODY"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Poké-BODY">Poké-BODY</span></h3>
<p>A <b>Poké-BODY</b> (Japanese: ポケボディー <i>Poké-Body</i>) is a type of <a href="#Pokémon_Power">Pokémon Power</a> that is active for as long as the <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon</a> that has it is in play. A Poké-BODY is sometimes reminiscent of that Pokémon's in-game <a href="/wiki/Ability" title="Ability">Ability</a>, such as <a href="/wiki/Ludicolo_(Secret_Wonders_13)" title="Ludicolo (Secret Wonders 13)">Ludicolo's Rain Dish</a> Ability. Poké-BODIES have a variety of different effects and can affect almost any aspect of gameplay.
</p>
<h3><span id="Pok.C3.A9-POWER"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Poké-POWER">Poké-POWER</span></h3>
<p>A <b>Poké-POWER</b> (Japanese: ポケパワー <i>Poké-Power</i>) is a type of <a href="#Pokémon_Power">Pokémon Power</a> that the player is able to use during their <a href="#Turn">Turn</a>. In a similar fashion to <a href="#Poké-BODY">Poké-BODIES</a>, Poké-POWERS can affect almost any aspect of gameplay, and can often be used once during the player's turn, before their <a href="#Attack">Attack</a>. Some can be used multiple times and some are designed to cause an after-effect to the <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon</a> with it being <a href="#Knock_Out">Knocked Out</a>.
</p>
<h3><span id="Pok.C3.A9mon_ex"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Pokémon_ex">Pokémon ex</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_ex_(TCG)" title="Pokémon ex (TCG)">Pokémon ex (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>Pokémon ex</b> (Japanese: <b>ポケモンex</b> <i>Pokémon ex</i>) are Pokémon with significantly higher <a href="#Hit_Points">Hit Points</a> compared to the majority of regular Pokémon. They were first introduced in the <a href="/wiki/Scarlet_%26_Violet_(TCG)" title="Scarlet & Violet (TCG)">Scarlet & Violet</a> <a href="#Expansion">expansion</a>, and can be Basic, Stage 1, or Stage 2 Pokémon. Similar to the <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon-ex_(TCG)" title="Pokémon-ex (TCG)">Pokémon-ex</a> released during the <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game#EX_Series" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">EX Series</a>, when a Pokémon-EX is defeated, the opponent takes two <a href="#Prize_card">Prize cards</a> instead of one.
</p>
<h3><span id="Pok.C3.A9mon-EX"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Pokémon-EX">Pokémon-EX</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon-EX_(TCG)" title="Pokémon-EX (TCG)">Pokémon-EX (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>Pokémon-EX</b> (Japanese: <b>ポケモンEX</b> <i>Pokémon EX</i>) are <a href="#Basic_Pokémon">Basic Pokémon</a> with significantly higher <a href="#Hit_Points">Hit Points</a> compared to the majority of regular Basic Pokémon. They were first introduced in the <a href="/wiki/Next_Destinies_(TCG)" title="Next Destinies (TCG)">Next Destinies</a> <a href="#Expansion">expansion</a>, replacing <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_LV.X_(TCG)" title="Pokémon LV.X (TCG)">Pokémon LV.X</a> <a href="#Pokémon_LEGEND">Legendary Pokémon</a>. Similar to the <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon-ex_(TCG)" title="Pokémon-ex (TCG)">Pokémon-ex</a> released during the <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game#EX_Series" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">EX Series</a>, when a Pokémon-EX is defeated, the opponent takes two <a href="#Prize_card">Prize cards</a> instead of one.
</p>
<h3><span id="Pok.C3.A9mon-GX"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Pokémon-GX">Pokémon-GX</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon-GX_(TCG)" title="Pokémon-GX (TCG)">Pokémon-GX (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>Pokémon-GX</b> were introduced in the <a href="/wiki/Sun_%26_Moon_(TCG)" title="Sun & Moon (TCG)">Sun & Moon</a> expansion. They are similar to Pokémon-EX, but with two main differences - they aren't always Basic Pokémon (for example, a Pokémon that is typically Stage 1 will have a Stage 1 Pokémon-GX) and they have access to special GX Attacks, which are very powerful but only one GX attack can be used per game. Like with Pokémon-EX, defeating a Pokémon-GX would net two Prize Cards.
</p><p><b>TAG TEAM Pokémon-GX</b> were introduced in the <a href="/wiki/Team_Up_(TCG)" title="Team Up (TCG)">Team Up</a> expansion. These depict pairs or sometimes trios of Pokémon, are always Basic, and are even more powerful than other Pokémon-GX, with HP ranging from 250 to 300, but defeating them nets three Prize Cards.
</p>
<h3><span id="Pok.C3.A9mon_LEGEND"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Pokémon_LEGEND">Pokémon LEGEND</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_LEGEND_(TCG)" title="Pokémon LEGEND (TCG)">Pokémon LEGEND (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>Legend cards</b> or <b>Legendary Pokémon</b> first appeared in <a href="/wiki/HeartGold_%26_SoulSilver_(TCG)" title="HeartGold & SoulSilver (TCG)">HeartGold & SoulSilver</a> <a href="#Expansion">expansion</a> as one of the two variants of <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_LV.X_(TCG)" title="Pokémon LV.X (TCG)">Pokémon LV.X</a>: the top half and the bottom half.  Both card halves use the same name, so each one counts toward the four card of the same name <a href="#Deck">deck</a> rule. Pokémon Legend cards cannot be played during setup, and both card halves must be played on the Bench at the same time.  The two cards count as one card while in play.
</p>
<h3><span id="Pok.C3.A9mon_Power"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Pokémon_Power">Pokémon Power</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Power_(TCG)" title="Pokémon Power (TCG)">Pokémon Power (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>Pokémon Powers</b> (Japanese: <b>特殊能力</b> <i>special ability</i>) are additional effects that the <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon card's</a> player can trigger once or multiple times during their <a href="#Turn">Turn</a>, before they <a href="#Attack">Attack</a>. Starting with <a href="/wiki/Expedition_Base_Set_(TCG)" title="Expedition Base Set (TCG)">Expedition Base Set</a> <a href="#Expansion">Expansion</a>, Pokémon Powers were split into two groups: <a href="#Poké-POWER">Poké-POWERS</a> and <a href="#Poké-BODY">Poké-BODIES</a>. Poké-POWERS are special effects that the player must trigger or announce using. A Poké-BODY's effect is one that is in effect regardless. Both, however, are still officially considered to be Pokémon Powers. With the release of the <a href="/wiki/Black_%26_White_(TCG)" title="Black & White (TCG)">Black & White</a> <a href="#Expansion">Expansion</a>, Pokémon Powers were combined into one mechanic once again and renamed <a href="#Ability">Abilities</a>.
</p>
<div id="AdThrive_Content_9_desktop" class="adthrive-ad adthrive-content adthrive-content-9 adthrive-ad-cls" style="min-height: 250px;"></div><h3><span id="Pok.C3.A9mon_V"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Pokémon_V">Pokémon V</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_V_(TCG)" title="Pokémon V (TCG)">Pokémon V (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>Pokémon V</b> (Japanese: <b>ポケモンV</b> <i>Pokémon V</i>) are <a href="#Basic_Pokémon">Basic Pokémon</a> with significantly higher <a href="#Hit_Points">Hit Points</a> compared to the majority of regular Basic Pokémon. They were first introduced in the <a href="/wiki/Sword_%26_Shield_(TCG)" title="Sword & Shield (TCG)">Sword & Shield</a> <a href="#Expansion">expansion</a>. Similar to <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon-EX_(TCG)" title="Pokémon-EX (TCG)">Pokémon-EX</a>, when a Pokémon V is Knocked Out, the opponent takes two <a href="#Prize_card">Prize cards</a> instead of one.
</p><p>Pokémon VMAX, Pokémon V-UNION, and Pokémon VSTAR are subcategories of Pokémon V.
</p>
<h4><span id="Pok.C3.A9mon_VMAX"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Pokémon_VMAX">Pokémon VMAX</span></h4>
<p><b>Pokémon VMAX</b>, representing the <a href="/wiki/Dynamax" title="Dynamax">Dynamax</a>, <a href="/wiki/Gigantamax" title="Gigantamax">Gigantamax</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Eternamax" title="Eternamax">Eternamax</a> mechanic from <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Sword_and_Shield" title="Pokémon Sword and Shield">Pokémon Sword and Shield</a>, evolve from their respective Pokémon V and feature boosted HP and more powerful attacks. When a Pokémon VMAX is Knocked Out, the opponent takes three <a href="#Prize_card">Prize cards</a> instead of one.
</p>
<h4><span id="Pok.C3.A9mon_V-UNION"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Pokémon_V-UNION">Pokémon V-UNION</span></h4>
<p><b>Pokémon V-UNION</b> is a unique type of Pokémon V, in which each Pokémon V-UNION comprises four different cards with the same name. To play a Pokémon V-UNION, the four cards that form that Pokémon must be assembled from the discard pile onto the Bench and played as one card. Pokémon V-UNION is a separate evolutionary stage from Basic or Evolved Pokémon. When a Pokémon V-UNION is Knocked Out, the opponent takes three <a href="#Prize_card">Prize cards</a> instead of one.
</p>
<h4><span id="Pok.C3.A9mon_VSTAR"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Pokémon_VSTAR">Pokémon VSTAR</span></h4>
<p><b>Pokémon VSTAR</b> evolve from their respective Pokémon V and feature boosted HP and more powerful attacks, as well as an exclusive mechanic called a <b>VSTAR Power</b>. VSTAR Powers can be attacks or Abilities, and only one VSTAR Power can be used only once per game. When a Pokémon VSTAR is Knocked Out, the opponent takes two <a href="#Prize_card">Prize cards</a> instead of one.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Resistance">Resistance</span></h3>
<p>If a <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon</a> has <b>Resistance</b> (Japanese: <ruby lang="ja">抵抗力<rp>(</rp><rt>ていこうりょく</rt><rp>)</rp></ruby> <i>Resistance</i>) to a certain type, it means that if it is <a href="#Attack">Attacked</a> by a Pokémon of that type, it will receive less <a href="#Damage">Damage</a>. While not exceedingly rare, Resistance isn't very common either — most Pokémon don't have any. An example of a Pokémon with Resistance is <a href="/wiki/Ditto_(Fossil_3)" title="Ditto (Fossil 3)">Ditto</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Fossil_(TCG)" title="Fossil (TCG)">Fossil</a> <a href="#Expansion">Expansion</a> set. An example of a Pokémon without is <a href="/wiki/Grimer_(Aquapolis_79)" title="Grimer (Aquapolis 79)">Grimer</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Aquapolis_(TCG)" title="Aquapolis (TCG)">Aquapolis</a> expansion. The <a href="/wiki/EX_Dragon_(TCG)" title="EX Dragon (TCG)">EX Dragon</a> expansion introduced some <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon-ex" class="mw-redirect" title="Pokémon-ex">Pokémon-ex</a> with two different Resistances on the same card, such as <a href="/wiki/Rayquaza_ex_(EX_Dragon_97)" title="Rayquaza ex (EX Dragon 97)">Rayquaza ex</a>. Resistances were initially fixed at -30 damage, meaning the Pokémon would take 30 less damage from an attack. Unlike Weakness, this rule was always printed on the card, either to the left of or above the Resistance-type in the form of "-30". From the <a href="/wiki/Diamond_%26_Pearl_(TCG)" title="Diamond & Pearl (TCG)">Diamond & Pearl</a> set to <a href="/wiki/Sword_%26_Shield_(TCG)" title="Sword & Shield (TCG)">Sword & Shield</a>, Resistances were always -20 damage (also printed on the cards) unless on a reprint of a <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon card</a> that originally had a -30 Resistance. With <a href="/wiki/Sword_%26_Shield_(TCG)" title="Sword & Shield (TCG)">Sword & Shield</a>, resistances are now -30 again.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Retreat_cost">Retreat cost</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Retreat_cost" class="mw-redirect" title="Retreat cost">Retreat cost</a></i></dd></dl>
<p>When a player wants to move their <a href="#Active_Pokémon">Active Pokémon</a> to the <a href="#Bench">Bench</a>, that player can <b>Retreat</b> (Japanese: にげる <i>Retreat</i>) that <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon</a>. Then, a Pokémon on the Bench must replace the previous Active Pokémon. Each Pokémon has a <b>Retreat Cost</b>: a specific number of <a href="#Energy_card">Energy</a> that must be discarded from the Pokémon being retreated in order to move it back to the Bench. Retreating can only be done once per <a href="#Turn">Turn</a>. If the player doesn't have the required amount of Energy attached to discard or doesn't have any Benched Pokémon, their Pokémon is unable to retreat. Some Pokémon have no Retreat Cost and thus can retreat for free; others have a Retreat Cost of between one and five <span typeof="mw:File"><span title=" "><img alt=" " src="https://archives.bulbagarden.net/media/upload/thumb/1/1d/Colorless-attack.png/20px-Colorless-attack.png" decoding="async" loading="lazy" width="20" height="20" class="mw-file-element" srcset="https://archives.bulbagarden.net/media/upload/thumb/1/1d/Colorless-attack.png/30px-Colorless-attack.png 1.5x, https://archives.bulbagarden.net/media/upload/thumb/1/1d/Colorless-attack.png/40px-Colorless-attack.png 2x" data-file-width="85" data-file-height="85"></span></span> Energies. Any type of Energy can be used for retreating, as any Energy can count as <a href="/wiki/Colorless_(TCG)" title="Colorless (TCG)">Colorless</a>.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Weakness">Weakness</span></h3>
<p>If a <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon</a> has <b>Weakness</b> (Japanese: <ruby lang="ja">弱点<rp>(</rp><rt>じゃくてん</rt><rp>)</rp></ruby> <i>Weakness</i>) to a certain <a href="#Type">type</a>, it means that if it is <a href="#Attack">attacked</a> by a Pokémon of that type, it will receive more <a href="#Damage">damage</a>. Most Pokémon have one Weakness, such as <a href="/wiki/Diglett_(Base_Set_47)" title="Diglett (Base Set 47)">Diglett</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Base_Set_(TCG)" title="Base Set (TCG)">Base Set</a>, but some have none, such as <a href="/wiki/Togepi_(Neo_Destiny_56)" title="Togepi (Neo Destiny 56)">Togepi</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Neo_Destiny_(TCG)" title="Neo Destiny (TCG)">Neo Destiny</a> <a href="#Expansion">Expansion</a> set. The <a href="/wiki/EX_Sandstorm_(TCG)" title="EX Sandstorm (TCG)">EX Sandstorm</a> expansion introduced some <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon-ex" class="mw-redirect" title="Pokémon-ex">Pokémon-ex</a> with two different Weaknesses on the same card, such as <a href="/wiki/Aggron_ex_(EX_Sandstorm_95)" title="Aggron ex (EX Sandstorm 95)">Aggron ex</a>. Weaknesses were initially fixed at ×2 damage, meaning the Pokémon would take twice the amount of damage dealt by an attack. Variable Weaknesses were later introduced in the <a href="/wiki/Diamond_%26_Pearl_(TCG)" title="Diamond & Pearl (TCG)">Diamond & Pearl</a> expansion, with Weaknesses of +10, +20, +30, +40 and ×2. Generally, with variable weaknesses, <a href="#Basic_Pokémon">Basic Pokémon</a> will have a Weakness of +10, Stage 1 Pokémon one of +20, and Stage 2 Pokémon one of +30, with a select few having one of +40. There is no general pattern of Pokémon with a ×2 Weakness; although, <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_SP_(TCG)" title="Pokémon SP (TCG)">Pokémon SP</a> always have a weakness of ×2. From <a href="/wiki/HeartGold_%26_SoulSilver_(TCG)" title="HeartGold & SoulSilver (TCG)">HeartGold & SoulSilver</a> expansion onwards, Weaknesses return to ×2.
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Trainer_card">Trainer card</span></h2>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Trainer_card_(TCG)" title="Trainer card (TCG)">Trainer card (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p>A <b>Trainer card</b> (Japanese: トレーナーズ <i>Trainer's</i>) is one of three main types of card found in the <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trading_Card_Game" title="Pokémon Trading Card Game">Pokémon Trading Card Game</a>, alongside <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon cards</a> and <a href="#Energy_card">Energy cards</a>. While Pokémon cards do the direct <a href="#Attack">Attacking</a> of an opponent's cards and Energy cards power their attacks, Trainers provide a more supportive role, allowing a player to search through their <a href="#Deck">deck</a>, draw cards, or other special effects. During a player's <a href="#Turn">Turn</a>, they may play a Trainer card from their hand, follow its instructions, and then typically <a href="#Discard_pile">discard it</a>.
</p>
<div id="AdThrive_Content_10_desktop" class="adthrive-ad adthrive-content adthrive-content-10 adthrive-ad-cls" style="min-height: 250px;"></div><h3><span class="mw-headline" id="ACE_SPEC">ACE SPEC</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/ACE_SPEC_card_(TCG)" title="ACE SPEC card (TCG)">ACE SPEC card (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>ACE SPEC</b> are powerful <a href="#Trainer_card">Trainer cards</a> with a special drawback: there can only be one ACE SPEC in a <a href="#Deck">deck</a>.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Item_card">Item card</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Item_card_(TCG)" title="Item card (TCG)">Item card (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p>The <b>Item card</b> (Japanese: グッズ <i>Goods</i>)  is the main type of <a href="#Trainer_card">Trainer card</a>. It was the first to be introduced, and was the only type of Trainer card until <a href="#Supporter_card">Supporter cards</a> and <a href="#Stadium_card">Stadium cards</a> were split into their own categories in the <a href="/wiki/Diamond_%26_Pearl_(TCG)" title="Diamond & Pearl (TCG)">Diamond & Pearl</a> <a href="#Expansion">Expansion</a> set. Unlike these two, Item cards have subtypes, and thus have a wide range of effects. The main subtype of Item card is <a href="/wiki/Trainer_card_(TCG)#Technical_Machine" title="Trainer card (TCG)">Technical Machines</a>, which include one additional <a href="#Attack">Attack</a> usable by the <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon</a> the card is attached to. Prior to the <a href="/wiki/Scarlet_%26_Violet_(TCG)" title="Scarlet & Violet (TCG)">Scarlet & Violet</a> Series, <a href="#Pokémon_Tool">Pokémon Tools</a> were also considered a subtype of Item cards. Other set-specific types, such as <a href="/wiki/Trainer_card_(TCG)#Goldenrod_Game_Corner" title="Trainer card (TCG)">Goldenrod Game Corner</a> and <a href="/wiki/Trainer_card_(TCG)#Rocket's_Secret_Machine" title="Trainer card (TCG)">Rocket's Secret Machine</a>, also exist. The <a href="/wiki/Boundaries_Crossed_(TCG)" title="Boundaries Crossed (TCG)">Boundaries Crossed</a> expansion introduced <a href="#ACE_SPEC">ACE SPEC</a> Trainer cards, really powerful cards with the drawback that there can only be one in a <a href="#Deck">deck</a>.
</p>
<h3><span id="Pok.C3.A9mon_Tool"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Pokémon_Tool">Pokémon Tool</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Tool_card_(TCG)" title="Pokémon Tool card (TCG)">Pokémon Tool card (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p><b>Pokémon Tools</b> (Japanese: ポケモンのどうぐ <i>Pokemon Tool</i>) are a type of <a href="#Trainer_card">Trainer card</a> that provide a special benefit to the <a href="#Pokémon_card">Pokémon</a> they are attached to. <a href="#Active_Pokémon">Active Pokémon</a> and <a href="#Bench">Bench Pokémon</a> may only have one Pokémon Tool attached to it, and it may not be removed unless specifically instructed. Prior to the <a href="/wiki/Scarlet_%26_Violet_(TCG)" title="Scarlet & Violet (TCG)">Scarlet & Violet</a> Series, Pokémon Tool cards were a special type of <a href="#Item_card">Item card</a>.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Stadium_card">Stadium card</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Stadium_card_(TCG)" title="Stadium card (TCG)">Stadium card (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p>A <b>Stadium card</b> (Japanese: スタジアム <i>Stadium</i>) is a type of <a href="#Trainer_card">Trainer card</a> and is designed to change an aspect of gameplay for both players. Unlike <a href="#Item_card">Item cards</a> and <a href="#Supporter_card">Supporter cards</a>, Stadium cards cause a long-term change in gameplay and may only be removed when another Stadium card is played. They are often played in order to help the player or hinder the opponent. For example, the <a href="/wiki/Battle_Frontier_(TCG)" class="mw-redirect" title="Battle Frontier (TCG)">Battle Frontier</a> Stadium card would not be used by players whose <a href="#Deck">decks</a> included Colorless-<a href="#Pokémon_type">type</a>, Darkness-type or Metal-type <a href="#Evolution_card">Evolved Pokémon</a>. A player can only play one Stadium card each <a href="#Turn">Turn</a> and cannot play a Stadium card with the same name as one already in play.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Supporter_card">Supporter card</span></h3>
<dl><dd><i>Main article: <a href="/wiki/Supporter_card_(TCG)" title="Supporter card (TCG)">Supporter card (TCG)</a></i></dd></dl>
<p>A <b>Supporter card</b> (Japanese: サポート <i>Support</i>) is a type of <a href="#Trainer_card">Trainer card</a>. Supporter cards are based on characters who are, more often than not, included in the <a href="/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_games" title="Pokémon games">video games</a>, such as <a href="/wiki/Lusamine_(Crimson_Invasion_96)" title="Lusamine (Crimson Invasion 96)">Lusamine</a>, <a href="/wiki/Professor_Rowan_(TCG)" class="mw-redirect" title="Professor Rowan (TCG)">Professor Rowan</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Clavell_(Paldea_Evolved_177)" title="Clavell (Paldea Evolved 177)">Clavell</a>. A player can only play <b>one</b> Supporter card each <a href="#Turn">Turn</a>, this is because they are usually very helpful to the player. Originally, Supporters stayed in play until the end of the player's turn, at which point they were discarded. Starting with <a href="/wiki/Black_%26_White_(TCG)" title="Black & White (TCG)">Black & White</a>, Supporter cards move directly to the discard pile after resolving their effect.
</p>
